analysis.notes: The jazz blues adds three things to the basic three-chord blues: a ii–V into bar 5 (Cm7–F7 → Bb7), a passing diminished chord in bar 6 (Bdim7, really a rootless G7b9) that leads back to F7, and a turnaround in bars 8–12 made of the iii–VI–ii–V chain (Am7–D7–Gm7–C7). The F7 is the tonic even though it is a dominant chord: that is the blues.

learning.why: Every jam session calls a blues. Twelve bars, one key, but it packs in secondary dominants, a passing diminished chord, and a turnaround: the whole vocabulary in miniature.
drills: Comp the twelve bars with 6th-string-root shells, then 5th-string, then alternate every bar.
Solo with the F blues scale for one chorus, then chord tones only for one chorus, then mix.
Play the 3rd of every chord on beat one, then the b7 on beat one.
Loop bars 9–12 and practise turnaround lines that land on the F on bar 1.
milestones: Comp shells through the form without looking
Comp drop-2 voicings with the trio
Play a chord-tone solo over the whole form
Play three choruses without repeating a phrase
